lesson.title: Grouping by Descent, Not by Looks: Cladistics
lesson.summary: Cladistics is a method of classifying organisms into groups, called clades, based strictly on shared derived characters inherited from a common ancestor, rather than on overall physical similarity.
lesson.body:
Cladistics is a specific, rigorous method for figuring out evolutionary relationships and building classifications that reflect those relationships as accurately as possible. Its central rule is easy to state but has far reaching consequences: organisms should be grouped together based on shared derived characters, traits that were newly evolved in a common ancestor and then inherited by all of that ancestor's descendants, rather than being grouped based on overall similarity in appearance. You will study shared derived characters in much greater technical detail in a later chapter, but the core idea needs to be introduced here because it is the foundation the entire method rests on.

To see why this rule matters, think back to convergent evolution. Streamlined body shape evolved independently in sharks, dolphins, and ichthyosaurs. If a classification method simply grouped organisms by overall physical resemblance, it might lump these three together as close relatives because they look alike, which would be a serious error, dolphins are mammals more closely related to cows and hippos than to sharks or ichthyosaurs, and their streamlined shape says nothing about that deeper relationship, it only reflects a shared way of moving through water. Cladistics was developed specifically to avoid this trap, by insisting that only traits inherited from a shared ancestor, not traits that merely look similar for other reasons, count as evidence of relatedness.

A cladistic classification is organized around the concept of a clade, defined as an ancestor and absolutely all of its descendants, no more and no fewer. A clade is sometimes described as monophyletic for exactly this reason, it captures a complete branch of the evolutionary tree with nothing left out and nothing extra included. This is a stricter standard than older, pre-cladistic classification schemes sometimes used, which occasionally grouped organisms by shared primitive traits retained from a distant ancestor, traits biologists call symplesiomorphies, or left out some descendants of a common ancestor because those descendants had evolved to look very different from their relatives. A well known example of that older kind of mistake is the traditional class Reptilia as it used to be defined, which excluded birds even though birds descended from within the reptile lineage, specifically from theropod dinosaurs. Because reptiles as traditionally defined excluded one entire branch of descendants, that grouping is not a true clade under cladistic standards, birds have to be included for the group to be monophyletic.

Determining which traits are truly shared derived characters, and therefore useful for building clades, requires a comparison point, which is where the idea of an outgroup comes in. An outgroup is a species or group known, from other evidence, to have branched off earlier than the group being studied, the ingroup. By comparing the ingroup's traits to the outgroup, biologists can tell which version of a trait is ancestral, shared with the outgroup, and which version is derived, a new trait found only within the ingroup, and therefore a candidate for identifying which members of the ingroup are more closely related to each other. You will use this outgroup comparison technique directly in the next chapter when you learn to build and read cladograms, the branching diagrams that are the visual output of a cladistic analysis.

It is worth connecting cladistics back to the arc of this unit as a whole. Every mode of speciation you studied, allopatric, sympatric, and the diversification patterns seen in adaptive radiation, produces exactly the kind of branching, ancestor-to-descendants history that cladistics is designed to reconstruct. Cladistics does not describe a different biological process from speciation, it is the analytical method biologists use, working backward from the traits organisms have today, to infer the pattern of splitting events that speciation left behind.
